title.narrative: Economic Recovery for Conflict Affected People - ERCAP
Economic Recovery for Conflict Affected People - ERCAP

description.narrative:
Overall goal
Enhanced economic adaptation, protection and recovery of conflict-affected populationsand other vulnerable community members, through an inclusive, innovative, gender- and conflict-sensitive, and climate-smart systems development approach.
Objectives/Outcomes
Through inclusive, market-based solutions, the programme is expected to influence systems change to enable the following:
Outcome 1: Conflict-affected communities have resilient livelihoods through improved productivity and production of targeted crops and livestock value chains, climate-smart systems and access to income-generating opportunities (self and wage work) through strengthening Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) through appropriate Business Development Services.
Outcome 2: Conflict-affected communities and MSMEs use a range of appropriate and affordable financial products, climate smart technologies, instruments to create and enhance livelihood opportunities through strengthened financial service providers' capacities as well as support to the target communities to have the required financial literacy and capability to utilise financial services.
Outcome 3: Vulnerable conflict-affected communities have improved capacity to mitigate and reduce protection risks through access to justice, community support mechanisms, and psychosocial support, including access to early recovery support protection capacity enhancement support across the displacement cycle.
The core of this proposed project is aimed at improving the economic adaptation, protection, and recovery of populations affected by conflict.
Övergripande syfte i det föreslagna projektet är att bidra till förbättrad ekonomisk återhämtning, reducera sårbarhet och bidra till återhämtning för människor som drabbats av konflikter.

sector.narrative: Education/training in banking and financial services

description.narrative:
In its second year of implementation (2025), ERCAP has launched a number of activities that are contributing to economy recovery in the targeted areas.
Key Change Processes: Market systems: Fee-for-service models are now functioning (farmers pay ETB 1,000/ha for tillage; private agrovets, feed suppliers, and tractor owners have re-entered and expanded). Input supply chains (seeds, veterinary drugs, feed, solar brooding) have been re-established through private B2B linkages.
Financial systems: FSPs (MFIs, SACCOs, banks) have increased risk appetite, introduced solidarity/group lending and digital products, and begun financing follow-on loans with their own capital. Sharia-compliant products have unlocked previously excluded demand.
Institutional roles: Government offices (agriculture, livestock, TVET, cooperatives) have begun shifting from direct service delivery to facilitation, regulation, and coordination.
Protection-economic nexus: Trauma-informed sequencing (MHPSS legal documentation finance/livelihoods) has improved retention and graduation for IDPs.
Key Changes in Attitude, Behaviour and Relations
Smallholder farmers and backyard breeders (especially returnees and women): Moved from beneficiary mindset expecting free/subsidised services to customer behaviour willingly paying for tillage, quality inputs, veterinary services, and modern hives; self-sourcing seeds and budgeting for them as normal business costs.
Private sector actors (tractor owners, agrovets, feed processors, job platforms): Increased commercial confidence; now investing their own capital, expanding geographic reach, and building B2B relationships instead of waiting for NGO subsidies.
Financial service providers and SACCOs: Shifted from risk-averse, collateral-focused lending to inclusive, data-driven, and solidarity-based products; now view women/youth/informal businesses and IDPs as viable clients.
Government institutions: Changed from parallel implementers to market facilitators/regulators (coordinating service schedules, embedding ToT models, adopting VSLA/protection approaches in routine work).
Women and IDPs: Increased leadership in VSLAs/cooperatives (women now 83% of VSLA members, holding key governance roles) and greater agency in negotiation, market engagement, and household decision-making. Relations between host/returnee/IDP communities have improved through joint economic activities and shared market spaces.
Target groups are now capable of doing things they were not capable of doing at the beginning of the intervention, such as
-Access and pay for timely mechanised tillage, quality veterinary drugs, modern beekeeping inputs, and commercial feed/energy solutions on market terms. -Obtain formal credit (solidarity loans, digital lending, SACCO finance) and repay on schedule without collateral. -Self-source inputs, budget commercially, and engage directly with buyers/off-takers (horticulture, honey, livestock). -Use hybrid job-matching platforms (digital call centre physical boards) to seek formal wage opportunities. -IDPs specifically can secure civil documentation, manage trauma through MHPSS, participate in VSLAs as financial and social safety nets, and launch petty-trade or vocational enterprises. -Women lead producer groups, negotiate B2B deals, and exercise greater economic decision-making power.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
